findings.title: No pooled QC samples in this file.
findings.detail: I couldn't find any pooled QC samples. Pooled QCs — an aliquot of every sample, mixed, injected every 5–10 samples — are the field's standard evidence that your run was stable, and reviewers increasingly expect them (Broadhurst et al. 2018, Metabolomics 14:72; mQACC 2022). Without them I can't compute QC-RSD, D-ratio, or drift correction. If QCs were run but aren't in this file, add them now; they cannot be reconstructed later. I looked at `feature_id` across all 396 rows, against the field's naming conventions for pooled QCs.
findings.why_it_matters: Without pooled QCs there is no measurement of technical variation, so QC-RSD filtering, the D-ratio and drift correction cannot be computed here — not by this app and not by any other tool from this file. That is a limit on what the analysis can claim, and it belongs in the methods section rather than in a footnote.

evidence.source: research/METABOLOMICS_PACK.md#Sample-role detection — the thing a generic tool cannot do

findings.title: There is no run order in this file, and half the quality diagnostics need one.
findings.detail: No column here is named as an injection or acquisition order, none parses as an acquisition timestamp, and none runs 1 to 396 with every position used exactly once. I looked at all 81 columns.
findings.why_it_matters: Instrument drift is often the largest single variance component in a run, and every way of seeing it is ordered by injection: drift diagnostics, QC-RLSC correction and the run-order overlay on the PCA scores plot all become impossible without one. The order is in the instrument's sequence file — if you still have it, adding the column now recovers all three.
findings.summary: No run-order column, so drift and QC-based corrections cannot be computed. No control for this yet.

findings.title: 80 numeric columns, but about 73 independent quantities.
findings.detail:
1 groups of columns move together at a Pearson correlation above 0.9 — 7 of the 80 numeric columns sit inside a group with at least one other, and the largest group holds 8. The biggest is `QC01`, `QC02`, `QC03`, `QC04` and 4 more. A compound count read off this table's width — 80 — overstates it by about 1.1×.

Clustered on correlation only, and the two things that leaves out pull opposite ways. The research clusters on near-identical retention time and correlation, and this table carries no retention time; supplying one could only split these groups and never merge them, which would raise the 73. Against that, every column here is observed often enough for its correlations to be computed, so nothing is counted as independent merely for want of overlap.
findings.why_it_matters: Untargeted features are not independent. One compound leaves the source as several ions — `[M+H]+`, `[M+Na]+`, `[M+K]+`, `[M+NH4]+` — and shows up again as its carbon-13 isotopologue, its dimer and its in-source fragments, all rising and falling together because they are the same molecules. Two numbers depend on which count you use: the one in the manuscript's data-description sentence, and the denominator of the multiple-testing correction. Nothing is collapsed here — merging features changes what is analyzed, and which member of a group represents the compound is a decision about the chemistry.
findings.summary: `80` numeric columns carry about `73` independent quantities. No control for this yet.

findings.title: `feature_id` names each row.
findings.detail: `feature_id` has `396` different values across `396` rows, one per row. A value that appears once cannot tell a model anything about a row it has not seen.
findings.why_it_matters: As a predictor it would be noise at best, and a way to memorize rows at worst.
findings.summary: `feature_id` is unique on every row: it names its row and is not a predictor.

findings.title: The wide shape is expected here.
findings.detail:
QC (8: QC01, QC02, QC03…); S0 (72: S002, S003, S004…).

These are different analytes, not one analyte measured several times. An untargeted panel names its features by mass and retention time, which reads as a numbered series to a general-purpose importer. Reshaping to long format would rebuild what a row is and is not what this table needs.
findings.why_it_matters: Wide repeated measures are fine for prediction, but if each row is a subject measured several times you may want one row per measurement instead — and clustered rows need a group-aware split.
findings.summary: The wide shape is expected for this kind of data; nothing needs changing.

findings.title: Your missing values cluster in the lowest-abundance features.
findings.detail: Across 396 features, a feature's missing rate tracks its abundance rank at a rank correlation of -0.97. 307 features have blanks; the highest rate is 55%, on one of the least abundant.
findings.why_it_matters: In metabolomics that usually means below the detection limit — left-censored rather than missing at random — and filling with a median would place non-detections in the middle of the distribution. Half the minimum observed is the convention, and it is the one a reader can check.

TurboTab recommends setting them to missing and reporting the count. TurboTab has not recoded them. 33 of `item_14`'s 300 answers are affected, and treating them as responses moves this item's mean by +0.655 — from 3.049 to 3.703 — which propagates into every scale score and every model. 4 other items carry the same shape: `item_22` (8, 8.0%, mean +0.399); `item_05` (9, 6.0%, mean +0.356); `item_33` (8, 5.0%, mean +0.247); `item_09` (7, 4.0%, mean +0.158).
findings.why_it_matters: A sentinel treated as a response is the worst kind of wrong number: it is inside the column's dtype, inside every plausibility check the app has, and it moves the item's mean, the scale score, every correlation the item enters and every coefficient downstream. Recoding is essential IF these are sentinels — and the app cannot know that they are, because some legitimate scales do run 0–9. Your codebook decides; the shift above is what the decision costs.
findings.summary: 5 items carry values outside the 1–5 response scale.

findings.title: 40 columns share one 5-point response scale.
findings.detail: Every value in them is one of [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The block runs `item_01` … `item_40`.
findings.why_it_matters: The order comes from the instrument, not from the data — which makes the encoding row-local: the number for a row depends on that row's own answer and on nothing else, so it is applied now rather than fitted inside the training folds. An encoding derived from the observed frequencies would be a different object, would have to be deferred, and would silently change meaning between cohorts.
findings.summary: `40` columns share one 5-point response scale; ordinal models are not in this version.

findings.title: `respondent_id` names each row.
findings.detail: `respondent_id` has `300` different values across `300` rows, one per row. A value that appears once cannot tell a model anything about a row it has not seen.
findings.why_it_matters: As a predictor it would be noise at best, and a way to memorize rows at worst.
findings.summary: `respondent_id` is unique on every row: it names a participant and is not a predictor.

findings.title: The wide shape is expected here.
findings.detail:
item (40: item_01, item_02, item_03…).

These are the items of one instrument, not one quantity measured several times. Items are combined by scoring the scale, which is a decision about the instrument, not by reshaping the table.
findings.why_it_matters: Wide repeated measures are fine for prediction, but if each row is a subject measured several times you may want one row per measurement instead — and clustered rows need a group-aware split.
findings.summary: The wide shape is expected for this kind of data; nothing needs changing.
